answer.stillOpen: The shape is decided; no numeric coefficient is. How strength-of-holding is derived from the record, and what it scales to, is implementation for the people and life owner. The requested test — spam one low-stakes interaction ten times in a day and prove it cannot edit a trait, against several independent reliability-relevant events over real game time — has not been run.
answer.summary: Answered, and lamontae has since decided the shape. ChatGPT's contract: a passing event does not directly change a core trait; a notable event contributes only if it is a genuinely distinct experience; a formative event can make a trait more movable and exceptionally support one step when durable later behaviour corroborates it. Repeated clicks, reopening a screen or asking the same thing ten times are not ten pieces of evidence, and reading a screen creates no pressure at all. Ordinary adult movement should emerge from independent evidence across months to years and, for broad traits, more than one context. Trait-specific reading: reliability can move fastest from repeated kept or broken commitments; sociability needs voluntary patterns rather than mere opportunity; conflict needs evidence beyond one grievance or relationship; risk must not globalise from one domain; deliberation is slowest and needs sustained cross-context decision behaviour. It also found two live defects: people-trait-pack.ts still carries 8 to 15 year settlesOver values labelled first-playable judgements, and trait-resistance.ts makes effective force equal event force plus a failed-attempt pressure count, so repeated attempts can eventually move a trait that independent experience never touched, while every successful prior move adds permanent future resistance. lamontae, 2026-09-22, agreed with the recommendation to replace both, and decided the band: 'it should just depend on how strongly that trait is to them' — resistance scales per person per trait with how deeply held that trait is in that individual, rather than a fixed band per trait name or one global curve.

notes: The mechanism is built and is not in question: resistance is read from the person's own chain of records, and failed attempts are recorded so pressure accumulates rather than each attempt being an independent roll. How it is computed is engineering and stays in the code.

What is deferred is only the numbers, which decide how a life feels. They are authored placeholders and are labelled as such in the file, so an answer replaces three numbers per trait and touches no code.

The build currently asserts both directions at once and that is the part most worth challenging: somebody recently shaken is easier to shift again, while every change already made adds a permanent cost, so each shift leaves them harder to move than the last time they settled.
question: How much has to happen to somebody before a disposition actually shifts? Specifically: how much should a single formative event be able to do on its own against how much accumulated repetition should be needed, roughly how long a value has to have stood before it counts as settled, and whether a person who has already changed once becomes easier or harder to change again.

sourcesChecked.source: src/simulation/people-trait-pack.ts, the movability numbers currently shipped
sourcesChecked.whatItDidNotSettle: Each trait declares what a settled value resists, how long it takes to settle, and what each prior change adds. Deliberation settles hardest over fifteen years, reliability soonest over eight, the rest between. Every one of those numbers was chosen to be plausible rather than researched, and nothing checks them against anything.

Establishes that resistance can be read from records alone, that an unobserved person is not movable at all, and that repeated pressure eventually carries where one attempt does not. It proves the mechanism behaves; it has nothing to say about whether the pace it produces resembles a life.

sourcesChecked.source: The owner's instruction of 2026-09-22: 'every character should be able to change with varying levels of resistance.'
sourcesChecked.whatItDidNotSettle: Settles that resistance must vary between people, which the record-chain reading delivers. It gives no sense of scale — whether a disposition should shift once in a decade or several times in a year.

title: What a believable pace of personality change looks like
usableAnswer: Rough scales rather than exact numbers: how many significant events, over how long, before a disposition plausibly moves; whether one severe event should ever be enough on its own; and a position on whether prior change makes the next change easier, harder, or both depending on how recent it was. Worked against any of the five current traits would be ideal, since they differ and should.
whyItMatters: These numbers are what a player actually feels. Set too loose, characters reinvent themselves every few months and stop being people. Set too tight, nothing anyone does to anyone ever matters and the system is decoration. Both failures look identical in tests, which all pass either way, so nothing in the repository will ever catch a wrong answer here.
